title: Naomi
author: Jun'ichirō Tanizaki
note: Tokyo, 1924. New English from the Japanese.

scenes.title: A Strange Marriage
scenes.reentry: I mean to set down, as honestly and as frankly as I can, the plain facts of the married life I share with my wife—a relationship that, I suspect, has few parallels anywhere.

breaths.text: I mean to set down, as honestly and as frankly as I can, the plain facts of the married life I share with my wife—a relationship that, I suspect, has few parallels anywhere.
For me it is a record I shall never forget, and precious; for my readers, I dare say, it will serve as a kind of reference.
Japan these days is growing more international by the hour.
Japanese and foreigners mix freely; every sort of doctrine and idea comes pouring in; men, of course, and women too, are turning Western at a clip.
In a climate like this, couples of our peculiar kind, once so rare, will surely start turning up all over.
Looking back, we were already odd from the start.
I first met the woman who is now my wife some eight years ago.
I no longer remember the month or the day, but at the time she was a waitress at a place called Café Diamond, near Kaminarimon in Asakusa.
She was barely fifteen by the old count.
When I came to know her she had only just entered service there, a complete novice—not a full waitress at all, only an apprentice: an egg of a waitress, if you like.
Why a man of twenty-eight should have fixed his eye on a child like that I cannot say even now, not clearly.
Probably, at first, it was the name that pleased me.
Everyone called her Nao-chan, but when I asked, her real name turned out to be Naomi.
That “Naomi” struck my curiosity hard.
Naomi—splendid, I thought.
Write it NAOMI in Roman letters and she might as well be a Westerner.
That was how it began, and from there I started watching her more closely.

Strange how it works: once the name is Western, the face itself starts looking a little foreign, and clever besides, and you find yourself thinking it is a waste to leave a girl like that serving in a place of that sort.

In fact Naomi’s face (I shall write her name in katakana from here on; otherwise the flavor is lost) had something of the motion-picture actress Mary Pickford about it, and was certainly Western-looking.
This is no mere fondness of mine.
Even now, as my wife, a great many people say the same, so it must be true.
And not the face alone: strip her bare and the body is still more Western—though of course I learned that later, and at the time I knew nothing of the kind.
I only guessed, vaguely, from the way she wore her clothes, that with a figure like that the arms and legs could not be badly made.
A girl of fifteen or sixteen is hard to read unless you are her own parent or sister.
Asked what Naomi’s nature was like in the café days, I cannot give a clear answer.
Naomi herself, I expect, would say she simply passed those months in a kind of daze.
From the outside she seemed, if anything, a gloomy, taciturn child.
Her complexion had a bluish cast, like pane after pane of colorless plate glass stacked together, a deep, sunken tint, and she did not look healthy.

Partly this was because she had only just come into service: she wore no powder, as the other waitresses did, and was still a stranger to customers and companions alike, so she kept small in a corner and worked in silence, fussing at this and that.
That may be why she struck me as clever, too.
I ought to say something of myself.
At the time I was an engineer at an electric company, drawing a salary of a hundred and fifty yen a month.
I was born near Utsunomiya in Tochigi, finished the local middle school, came up to Tokyo and entered the Higher Technical School at Kuramae, and became an engineer not long after graduating.
Except on Sundays I commuted every day from a lodging-house in Shibaguchi to the company in Ōimachi.
Living alone in lodgings on a hundred and fifty yen a month, I was fairly comfortable.
I was the eldest son, but I had no duty to send money home to my mother or brothers and sisters.
The family farm was a sizable concern; my father was already gone, but my aged mother and a loyal uncle and aunt ran everything, so I was entirely free.
That did not mean I dissipated myself.
I was, if anything, a model salaried man—frugal, earnest, so ordinary as to be almost without character, going through the day’s work with neither complaint nor discontent.
That, more or less, was how I was then.
At the company, “Kawai Jōji” had a reputation as a “gentleman. ”
My amusements, such as they were, amounted to going to the motion pictures of an evening, strolling Ginza-dōri, or, on a rare splurge, the Imperial Theatre.
I was a young man not yet married, of course, and I did not dislike the company of young women.

Raised in the country, I was clumsy with people and had no dealings with the other sex at all, which is probably how I got myself made into a “gentleman”; but if the surface was gentlemanly, the inside was anything but off its guard.
Walking the streets, riding the streetcar every morning, I kept a constant eye on women.
It was at just such a period that this person called Naomi happened to appear before me.
I had not, even then, decided that no one was more beautiful than Naomi.
Among the young ladies one passed in the streetcars, in the corridors of the Imperial Theatre, on Ginza-dōri, there were, needless to say, any number more beautiful than she.
Whether Naomi’s looks would improve was a question for the future; a slip of a girl of fifteen was both a pleasure and a worry to look ahead upon.
So my first plan was simply this: take the child in and look after her, and if she seemed promising, educate her thoroughly, and I might even take her as my wife.
That was about the extent of it.
Partly this was sympathy; partly I wanted a little change in a life too ordinary, too monotonous, a day-to-day existence.
Honestly, I had grown tired of years of lodging-house living, and I wanted somehow to add a point of color, a little warmth, to that bleak life.
Even a small house of my own—furnish a room, plant flowers, hang a birdcage on a sunny veranda—and keep a maid for the kitchen work and the dusting: how would that be?
And if Naomi came, she would serve as maid and as the bird as well.
That, more or less, was the idea.
If that was all, why not take a proper wife from a respectable family and make a formal household?
The truth is I had not yet the courage to marry.
I must go into this a little.
I am a common-sense sort of man, I dislike the eccentric, and I could not have managed it anyway; and yet, oddly, my views on marriage were quite advanced, quite Western.
“Marriage,” to most people, is a stiff, ceremonial affair.
First there is a go-between, sounding out both sides.
Then a miai.
If neither party objects, a formal matchmaker is appointed, betrothal gifts are exchanged, and the bride’s luggage—five loads, seven, thirteen—is carted to the groom’s house.
Then the procession, the honeymoon, the bride’s first visit home... a great deal of troublesome procedure, and I disliked all of it.
If I married, I wanted something simpler, freer.
At that time, had I wanted to marry, there would have been plenty of candidates.

I was a country fellow, but I was sturdy, my conduct was correct, and—funny to say it—my looks were ordinary enough, and I had the company’s confidence, so anyone would have been glad to arrange a match.
But the truth is I hated being “arranged.
” No matter how beautiful the woman, one or two meetings could never tell you a person’s spirit or nature.
To settle a companion for life on a passing feeling—“well, she’ll do,” “she’s rather pretty”—is a piece of folly no one should be capable of.
From that point of view, taking in a girl like Naomi, watching her grow at leisure, and then, if she pleased me, making her my wife, was the best method.
I did not want a rich man’s daughter or a woman of great education; this would do.

Besides, to make a friend of a young girl, to watch her develop morning and evening, and to live in a house together in a bright, easy, almost playful spirit, seemed to me a different interest from founding a proper household, and a special one.
In short, Naomi and I would play at house, innocently.
Not “setting up a household” in that bothersome sense, but an easy simple life.
That was what I wanted.

The Japanese “home” of today insists that a chest of drawers, a long brazier, floor cushions, and so on, must stand in their appointed places; the work of master, wife, and maid is divided with a nasty neatness; neighbors and relatives are a nuisance; extra expense piles up; what might be simple becomes complicated and cramped; and for a young salaried man it is neither pleasant nor good.
In that respect I believed my plan was, in its way, an idea.
I spoke of this to Naomi about two months after I first knew her.
In the interval I went to Café Diamond whenever I had time, making as many chances as I could to grow close to her.
Naomi was very fond of motion pictures, so on my days off we would look in at the theatre in the park, and on the way back stop at some little Western restaurant or a soba shop.
Even then she was a girl of few words, and you could never tell whether she was pleased or bored; she sat mostly in a sulk.
And yet when I invited her she never said no.
“Yes, I don’t mind going,” she would answer meekly, and follow me anywhere.
What she took me for, what she meant by coming along, I did not know; but she was still a real child, and she had not yet learned to turn a suspicious eye on “a man.
” This “uncle” took her to the pictures she liked and treated her now and then, so she went out to play with him: that, I imagined, was the whole of her simple, innocent feeling.
As for me, I asked of her then nothing more than to be a child’s companion, a kind and gentle “uncle,” and I showed nothing more in my manner.
When I think of those pale, dreamlike days, it is as if we had lived in a fairy tale, and even now I cannot help wishing we might be that innocent pair again.
“How is it, Naomi-chan?
Can you see? ”
When the picture-house was packed and there were no seats, we would stand in a row at the back, and I would often speak to her like that. Then Naomi would say, “No, I can’t see a thing,”
and stretch on tiptoe for all she was worth, trying to peek between the necks of the people in front.
“You won’t see that way.
Climb up on this wood here and hold on to my shoulder. ”
I would boost her from below and set her on the high rail of the barrier.
